Premier League Guide

Published 5 September 2026 Premier League TV96 Live Editorial Team Evergreen guide · 4 min read
Back to News & Guides

Following the Premier League becomes more rewarding when you look beyond the weekend's most discussed result. Twenty clubs can be pursuing very different objectives in the same round: a title challenge, a European place, a stronger mid-table finish or survival. The table connects those stories, but the schedule and individual match situations explain how they develop.

This is a guide to following the competition as a supporter. If you first need the basic rules, How the Premier League Works explains the 38-match season, points and final positions in detail.

Where the competition fits

The Premier League is the top division of English league football. The competition began in 1992, but English top-flight football existed long before that. Records described as Premier League records therefore cover a different period from records for the whole history of the English first division.

That distinction helps when reading historical comparisons. A club can have a major pre-1992 history which is invisible in a Premier League-only total. Neither dataset is necessarily wrong; they answer different questions. Check the time period before turning a statistic into a claim about all-time achievement.

The season's framework

Each of the 20 clubs faces the other 19 at home and away. Wins earn three points and draws one. The best final table position wins the league, while the bottom three move to the Championship. European places depend on the applicable allocation and cup outcomes.

Although the league schedule is balanced by the end, it is rarely balanced at every intermediate moment. Clubs can have played different numbers of home matches, faced different levels of opposition, or had a fixture postponed. Those differences matter most when judging a short run.

Build a useful matchweek routine

Before a round, identify the fixtures involving clubs near one another in the table. A meeting between direct rivals can change both teams' positions at once. Then note games in hand and the fixtures immediately before or after European or cup commitments.

After a round, separate the result from the performance description. A 1–0 win tells you the points award; it does not tell you whether the winner controlled the match, survived pressure or converted its only clear chance. A report becomes more useful when it explains how the score developed.

Finally, revisit the table with the completed results. Check whether an apparent leap reflects one club playing earlier than its rivals. A Saturday position may be provisional until the rest of the round is complete.

Read form without losing context

A five-match form sequence is a quick summary, not a complete assessment. Three wins against struggling opponents and three wins against leading sides produce the same points but may suggest different things about the next challenge.

Home and away patterns can also matter. Consider an invented team that wins four home matches but loses four away. Its overall return is 12 points from eight games, yet predicting its next match without considering the venue ignores a visible pattern. That pattern is evidence to investigate, not a guarantee that it will continue.

Where a reliable source provides expected goals, use it to examine chance quality over a defined sample. Do not combine incompatible providers or use an isolated number to dismiss the actual result.

Three races within one table

At the top, compare the points gap with the number of matches remaining. Around the European boundary, keep track of domestic cups and UEFA allocation changes. Near the bottom, ask how many clubs remain within reach and how their schedules interact.

Our European qualification guide explains why an exact qualifying position can change. The relegation guide explains why a familiar survival target is not a fixed rule. These distinctions prevent a table graphic from becoming an unsupported prediction.

What to notice in a match

Watch how a team advances the ball when the opposition presses. Does it find a free midfielder, play around the pressure through a full-back, or send a longer pass towards a forward? The answer can reveal the main contest even before a goal is scored.

Then watch what happens after possession is lost. A team committing many players forward may create chances while leaving space for counters. A side defending deeper can surrender possession without surrendering equally dangerous opportunities. Possession percentage alone cannot settle which plan is working.

Using TV96 Live

Open Matches and select the available Premier League filter to follow the relevant fixtures. On Standings, check the selected competition and games-played column before comparing clubs. Data can be delayed, and official competition information should resolve unusual tiebreaks or administrative decisions.

Use those pages together: the fixtures show where points were earned and where the next opportunities lie, while the table shows the accumulated outcome. That combination gives a more useful weekly picture than treating the latest headline as the entire season.
